mcq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{The convolution of two functions } f(t) \text{ and } g(t) \text{ in the context of Fourier transforms is defined as:}\)

\(\text{Given } f(t) = \begin{cases} 1, & 0 \leq t \leq 3 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \text{ and } g(t) = \begin{cases} 1, & 0 \leq t \leq 2 \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \text{ what is } (f*g)(t) \text{ for } 2 \leq t < 3?\)
\(\text{If } F\{f(t)\} = F(s) \text{ and } F\{g(t)\} = G(s), \text{ then according to the convolution theorem:}\)

mcq.OPT_1: \(\text{The convolution of } f(t) \text{ and } g(t)\)
mcq.OPT_2: \(\text{The sum of } f(t) \text{ and } g(t)\)
mcq.OPT_3: \(\text{The product of } f(t) \text{ and } g(t)\)
mcq.OPT_4: \(\text{The difference of } f(t) \text{ and } g(t)\)
mcq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{The inverse Fourier transform of the product } F(s)G(s) \text{ is:}\)
\(\text{For two rectangular pulses of equal width } a, \text{ the convolution results in a:}\)

sq.ANSWER:
Upto the stepMarks

\(\text{Convolution: } (f*g)(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) g(x-t) dt\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{Theorem: } F[f*g] = F[f] \cdot F[g]\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{Proof: } F[f*g] = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} (f*g)(x) e^{i s x} dx\)

(1 Mark)

\(= \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) g(x-t) e^{i s x} dt dx\)

(1 Mark)

\(\text{Change variable } u=x-t, dx=du, x=u+t\)

(1 Mark)

\(= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) e^{i s t} dt \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} g(u) e^{i s u} du = F(s) G(s)\)

(1 Mark)
sq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{Define convolution of two functions. State and prove the convolution theorem for Fourier transforms.}\)

sq.ANSWER:
Upto the stepMarks

\(\text{Let } F(s) = \frac{1}{1+is}, G(s) = \frac{1}{2+is}\)

(1 Mark)

\(\text{We know } f(x) = e^{-x} u(x), g(x) = e^{-2x} u(x) \text{ where } u(x) \text{ is unit step}\)

(2 Mark)

\(\text{By convolution theorem, inverse of } F(s)G(s) \text{ is } (f*g)(x)\)

(1 Mark)

\((f*g)(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) g(x-t) dt = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{0}^{x} e^{-t} e^{-2(x-t)} dt \text{ for } x>0\)

(2 Mark)

\(= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-2x} \int_{0}^{x} e^{t} dt = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-2x} (e^{x} - 1)\)

(1 Mark)

\(= \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} (e^{-x} - e^{-2x}) \text{ for } x>0, \text{ and 0 for } x<0.\)

(1 Mark)
sq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{Use convolution theorem to find the inverse Fourier transform of } \frac{1}{(1+is)(2+is)}.\)

lq.ANSWER:
StepMarks
The convolution of f(x) and g(x) is: \((f * g)(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(t) g(x-t) dt\)(3)
Properties: Commutative \(f*g = g*f\), Associative, Distributive(2)
Convolution theorem: \(\mathcal{F}\{f * g\} = \mathcal{F}\{f\} \cdot \mathcal{F}\{g\}\)(3)
Equivalently: \(\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{F(s)G(s)\} = f(x) * g(x)\)(2)
lq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{Define convolution of two functions } f(x) \text{ and } g(x). \text{ State the convolution theorem for Fourier transforms.}\)

lq.ANSWER:
StepMarks
Let \(F(s) = \frac{1}{a+is} \cdot \frac{1}{b+is}\)(1)
We know: \(\mathcal{F}\{e^{-ax}u(x)\} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \cdot \frac{1}{a+is}\) where \(u(x)\) is unit step(3)
Similarly: \(\mathcal{F}\{e^{-bx}u(x)\} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} \cdot \frac{1}{b+is}\)(3)
By convolution theorem: \(\mathcal{F}^{-1}\{F(s)\} = \sqrt{2\pi} [e^{-ax}u(x) * e^{-bx}u(x)]\)(2)
Compute convolution: \((e^{-ax}u(x) * e^{-bx}u(x)) = \int_{0}^{x} e^{-at} e^{-b(x-t)} dt\) for \(x > 0\)(3)
\(= e^{-bx} \int_{0}^{x} e^{(b-a)t} dt = e^{-bx} \left[ \frac{e^{(b-a)t}}{b-a} \right]_{0}^{x}\)(3)
\(= \frac{e^{-ax} - e^{-bx}}{b-a}\) for \(x > 0\), and \(0\) for \(x < 0\)(3)
lq.QUESTION_DESC: \(\text{Using convolution theorem, find the inverse Fourier transform of } \frac{1}{(a+is)(b+is)}.\)
